proposals.relationship: Stoler identifies Said’s Orientalism as a formative resource for thinking about colonial governance and the continuing politics of knowledge.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2015 interview, first answer, recalls reading Orientalism while writing her dissertation in Paris in 1978 and says Said and Foucault have differently informed thirty years of work. Her following answers insist that Said’s political project should not be reduced to literary criticism or separated from The Question of Palestine. This records her retrospective interpretation; neither Said book nor Stoler’s complete monographs is newly read.
primary_locators: 2015 interview, first answer beginning “I was initiated”; following answers on Orientalism and The Question of Palestine

proposals.relationship: Stoler credits Foucault’s analysis of subordination and his ethics of discomfort as continuing resources for her research while retaining her criticisms of his limits.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2015 interview explicitly recalls reading Volonté du savoir alongside Orientalism during dissertation work and says both informed her subsequent work. Answers on Marx and discomfort explain micro-sites of subsumption and vigilance toward ready-made categories. Her stated criticisms of Foucault remain, including existing edge_386. The interview’s parenthetical 1980 English manifestation is not treated as the date of the recalled 1978 reading; exact language or copy is not established. No cited original newly read.
primary_locators: 2015 interview, first answer; answers beginning “I’m often asked” and “I don’t think any of us”; later exegetical-reading answer

proposals.relationship: Stoler says Marx continues to inform her understanding of exploitation and subordination rather than having been displaced by Foucault.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2015 answer explicitly rejects a simple turn from Marx to Foucault, distinguishing Marx’s subsumption from Foucault’s leverage on its micro-sites. She gives feminism equal importance and relates these resources to plantation labor, gender and family arrangements. This bounded retrospective debt names no particular Marx title and does not subsume her work under a single school.
primary_locators: 2015 interview, answer beginning “I’m often asked” through the following plantation-labor paragraphs

proposals.relationship: Stoler uses Wittgenstein’s rough ground as a resource for investigating concept formation and subject formation in their messy settings.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2015 answer on fieldwork in philosophy invokes rough ground to reject remaining in transcendental abstraction and to ask how concepts and subjects form. It is a specific conceptual use, not proof of general discipleship, a direct quotation checked in a Wittgenstein original, or a claim about the whole of her method. The interview’s adjacent “Austen” attribution remains unresolved and is not silently corrected.
primary_locators: 2015 interview, answer beginning “Exegetical readings of Foucault,” paragraph beginning “Wittgenstein put it somewhat differently”

proposals.relationship: Stoler criticizes the silence around race in Bourdieu’s account of French bourgeois and middle-class distinction while acknowledging his engaged intellectual practice.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2015 fieldwork-in-philosophy answer says Bourdieu did not go far enough and specifies a silent corridor around race in the making of Distinction. This is her particular criticism, alongside acknowledgment that he was an engaged intellectual, rather than a dismissal of all his work. Neither Distinction nor an original reply is newly read; no reciprocal answer is claimed.

proposals.relationship: Stoler adapts de Certeau’s displaced history to examine contrary and disqualified narratives within colonial archives.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2007 article opening and note 7 explicitly take up displaced history but qualify the borrowing: Stoler’s use is closer to Foucault’s relation between erudite and disqualified knowledge than to de Certeau’s own definition. She therefore does not simply reproduce his concept. Note 7 identifies Heterologies (1986), “The Theater of the Quiproquo: Alexandre Dumas,” 151, and the Foucault text in the jointly edited Dirks–Eley–Ortner reader. That editorial credit is not a separate personal debt. Cited originals and the complete 2009 book remain unread.
primary_locators: 2007 publisher HTML, opening paragraph beginning “For Pramoedya, the tremors,” and note 7

proposals.relationship: Stoler uses Ricœur’s account of Aristotle’s distinction between history and poetry to frame her inquiry into colonial imaginaries that move between actual and possible events.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2007 paragraph on developing historical negatives invokes Ricœur’s parse of historians’ things that have been and poets’ things that might be, then explains that her ethnographic history moves between fictive, futuristic and concrete. Note 8 cites Time and Narrative, volume 1, Chicago 1984, especially 40–41. The distinction is a resource she works across, not a rule she simply endorses. Neither Ricœur nor Aristotle original newly read; no complete Stoler monograph reading.
primary_locators: 2007 publisher HTML, opening paragraph beginning “Because imagining what might be,” and note 8

proposals.relationship: Stoler explicitly takes Farge’s warning against easy archival familiarity as a resource for reading the fixed formats and apparent obviousness of colonial records.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2007 “Archival Conventions” opens with Farge’s warning and says she takes it to heart before specifying the clichéd formats and partial overviews of Netherlands Indies administrative writing. Notes 5 and 10 identify Le goût de l’archive (Paris 1989) and 90. Note 5 separately credits Farge’s material sensations and Steedman’s longings to animate archival relics; their contributions are not conflated. Farge’s original and Stoler’s complete monograph remain unread.
primary_locators: 2007 publisher HTML, “Archival Conventions,” opening quotation and next three paragraphs; notes 5 and 10

proposals.relationship: Ottevaere compares Stoler and Joan Scott as historians who question inherited categories rather than taking them as stable starting points.
proposals.evidence_note: Ottevaere’s complete 2004 review, paragraph after discussion of chapters 4 and 5, explicitly compares the careful evaluation of historically designated categories and caution about assumed colonial divisions. This is the named reviewer’s methodological comparison, not direct transmission, personal collaboration or Stoler’s own declaration of a Scott debt. It makes explicit the personal comparison already mentioned within group contribution edge_1218 without replacing that broader gender-history route. Neither original author’s complete monograph newly read.
primary_locators: 2004 H-Women review, paragraph beginning “The chapters give short illustrations”
